Lunar Stone Run · PP-1 rover picker

Pick a landing zone (south pole, Chandrayaan-3, Apollo 11 or Mare Crisium) and drive PP-1 from the Moon base. You have 2 minutes to pick at least 5 stones: park with a stone 1–2 m in front and press E. The claw reaches the stone using inverse kinematics, with a slow-motion, stop-motion close-up and a 3D scan. Sun and Earth positions are real (JPL DE421); the terrain and stones are simulated. Every stone counts toward the fleet goal of 100,000.

Introducing PP-1 Polaris Prospector

A practical south pole rover concept from Team Polaris Path, modelled on NASA's VIPER and Perseverance. It has four independently suspended, steerable wheels; vertical solar panels for the grazing polar Sun; a camera mast with LIDAR and floodlights for shadowed craters; a 1 m core drill; a front wire-mesh sample cage that fills stone by stone (12 stones), is set down on the ground as a depot when full, and is replaced by an empty one; and a 5-joint arm ending in a NASA JPL-style microspine gripper (hundreds of steel micro-spines that hook into the rock surface) that can lift rocks up to about 35 cm. Figures are design estimates, not flight hardware. Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, click a part to highlight it.

Science return at your landing site

Battery charge over the mission (cyan). Gold bands are sunlit hours. In the dark the rover runs 200 W survival heaters on battery.

Assumptions: three vertical panels giving 450 W in sunlight (similar to VIPER's class), a 6 kWh battery, an average driving speed of 0.1 m/s (0.36 km/h), about 3 rocks picked per arm-hour, and a 1 m core every 2 drilling hours.

Why is the south pole so hard?

The Moon's axis is tilted only 1.5° to the Sun, so at the pole the Sun never climbs more than about two degrees. It skims the horizon all day, every day. A small hill can block it for days, and a crater floor may never see it at all. Those dark floors are where the water ice is.

Earth hangs almost fixed in the lunar sky, wobbling a few degrees (libration). Near the pole that wobble decides whether a lander can talk home directly or needs a relay.

Data and method

Sun and Earth positions come from the JPL DE421 planetary ephemeris (the same family used by Horizons), with the Moon's real orientation (librations). They are precomputed every 2 hours for 2027–2028 and transformed to local horizon coordinates for any latitude and longitude in your browser.

Local horizons are modeled masks shaped to each site's setting (rim, massif, crater floor). Next step: replace them with LOLA-derived horizon masks from LROC Quickmap / Moon Trek. Site coordinates are approximate.

Design references for PP-1

Each PP-1 part is our own 3D model (rendered in this app), with a link to the real hardware that inspired it. We link to the originals instead of copying their photos.
